  <h1 class="advent-day-title">How does text become tokens?</h1>
  <p class="advent-day-lead">The model does not manipulate sentences exactly as we read them. Before computation, text must be split into discrete units: <strong>tokens</strong>.</p>
</div>

## The question

How does a tokenizer turn a character string into discrete units?

## The core idea

A **tokenizer** applies segmentation rules to a character string and produces an ordered sequence of *tokens*. A token is a unit in the tokenizer's vocabulary. Depending on its method and vocabulary, it may correspond to a whole word, part of a word, a character, or a sequence of bytes.

A token should therefore not be assumed to be a readable word. Segmentation depends on the tokenizer: two tokenizers may split the same string differently.

## A segmentation example

With a toy tokenizer, the string “cat follows the cat” might become:

<div class="advent-tokenization-example" aria-label="The text cat follows the cat is segmented into four tokens">
  <div class="advent-tokenization-source">“cat follows the cat”</div>
  <span aria-hidden="true">↓</span>
  <div class="advent-tokenization-tokens"><code>cat</code><code>follows</code><code>the</code><code>cat</code></div>
  <p>An ordered sequence of four tokens</p>
</div>

Another tokenizer might split some words into subword units. For a shorter string, one might produce `cat | follows`, while another produces `ca | t | follows`. The two segmentations represent the same original string, but they do not produce the same token sequence.

## Check yourself

Two tokenizers segment the same string differently:

- the first produces `["cat", "follows"]`;
- the second produces `["ca", "t", "follows"]`.

Have they necessarily produced the same token sequence?

<details class="advent-answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The two segmentations differ, even though they start from the same string. The split depends on the tokenizer and its vocabulary; we need to know which tokenizer was used to interpret the sequence.

</details>

## What this step does not do yet

Tokenization produces discrete units. It does not by itself provide the integer IDs consumed by the model. Mapping each token to a *token ID* is the subject of **day 4**. Using those IDs to select vectors from an embedding matrix comes next.

## Takeaway

Tokenization turns a character string into an ordered sequence of discrete units. A token is not necessarily a word, and segmentation depends on the tokenizer.
